text:
I write this from a plane somewhere over the Pacific. Life does this but once in a decade. There are certain divine convergences of events where the window to act is but a pinhole in the spirit realm. There will always be other opportunities. Lower-hanging fruit. Lesser partners will cross your path. Spiritually thin people. Easier people perhaps, yet depth will never be fully met.

What is truly coveted only opens for a short window. Hesitate, and the window closes forever. Risk it all and step through with all that you are, and enter an aligned life with everything you ever wanted and more. Maybe you fail in cataclysmic fashion. At least you can live with yourself that you really went for it.

Inner peace is earned by going for it when it matters. We all wish for serenity.

My alarm goes off at 3:45 AM just outside of Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport. I hesitated in October 2017. I know the pain of having an aligned life taken away by my own doing. Today, I’m going for it with everything that I am.

Her.

Maybe this could only happen after I let go of the people movies warned us about. The types of people we imagine watching us when we make life choices that aren’t fully proven yet. My brother once told me that no one watches movies anymore, and society is missing out on their lessons.

I watched The Fellowship of the Ring (2001) and Frozen (2013) on the 11-hour flight. A similar hidden warning repeats across different genres.

Good versus evil is a mere distraction while another darkness lurks in the shadows:

The townspeople.

They don’t get the same condemnation the bad guys get. But they’re certainly not the good guys either. They get a pass, because they’re meek. And we falsely associate meekness with good. Maybe it took a crisis to learn that the townspeople never stood for me, because they never stood for anything themselves.

Over the years, I’ve collected these types of people in my life. Maybe I was drawn to a version of them who once believed. Maybe they were drawn to my vitality. Townspeople are heartwarming at first. Their living rooms are comfortable, and they have family portraits on the walls. They work hard and send their children to good schools. They’re proud of their towns.

Outwardly, they just want the best for their families and communities. They own businesses where their children pop in after school. They’re the presidents of clubs and organizations. They show their face at local events. But inwardly, you can sense that something is not quite right. They’re seething. At a certain point, it hits you that under their lukewarm mask, they’re quietly rooting against you.

They’re fear-motivated and suspicious. The minute you don’t fit their delicate mold of an upstanding citizen, the minute you’re no longer useful to them, they turn against you. When things inevitably work out again, they shake their heads in disbelief: Dumb luck. Privilege. Access they never had.

They can never be happy for you because they know in their hearts they never went for it themselves. They have to reframe your perseverance to avoid their inner truth:

They’re cowards who took the safe, lesser path precisely when it mattered. We’ve all taken lesser paths. But there are certain windows. Certain divine convergences. Certain pinholes in the spirit realm.

And in those moments, the choice matters.

Having an intentional ordinary life does not mean you’re the townspeople cinema warns us about. I’m describing people who have a proclivity towards suspicion and hide their jealousy under performative modesty. People who see the outside world as a threat to their way of life. People who see really going for it as wrong, because it does not fit their tall poppy syndrome worldview.

I see their small-town preservationist accounts on X. The accounts that played into the fear that infiltrated the world after 2020. They’ll post an image of a quaint New England town with a church steeple and an old schoolhouse with the caption: “Enjoy it while it still lasts.” I want to shake them and say that in 50 years, your small town will look exactly the same. I, too, grew up in a town in Vermont of 820 people. The historical postcards from 1910 show the same houses, only with fields instead of forest. Ain’t nobody taking your life away from you.

If people like you can access it, it’s not coveted.

The townspeople are not your friends. They were never your friends. Watch the eyes of the Hobbit villagers when Gandalf comes with fireworks. Watch the eyes of the townspeople when Elsa accidentally reveals her powers at the coronation. When you announce a big life change, watch the eyes in the towns you live in and grew up in. The gears turn in their minds: You must be independently wealthy to do something like that.

They’re not thinking about you. They’re thinking about themselves.

This gets down to the root of what cinema is. Cinema is created by the great artists of the world to uplift people from the lukewarm abyss of a deeply trodden path. Cinema is meant to touch the outlier children coerced into deeply trodden paths by their families, teachers, and communities.

Reality can be punctured.

You need only relentless perseverance and unwavering hope that things will work out. And a spiritual fortitude to protect your energy from cynicism. Cynicism that starts when the 25-year-old alcoholics complain about the death of the middle class. That their degree no longer gets them a high-paying desk job with a 90s suburban utopia, and a romantic partner.

It’s sad to see young people fall into the political abyss while watching their own life pass them by.

The Internet is full of articles catering to the townspeople: “It’s impossible to live a middle-class life these days.” “The right or the left is responsible.” “We’re headed to a dystopian reality.” “We live in a cultural desert.” “Our education system is failing.” “Our quaint small towns are under threat from outsiders.”

If you’ve ever seen Edward Scissorhands (1990), the most dystopian reality has always been the fear-based plane of consciousness that inhabits suburban life. I spent part of my childhood in a Massachusetts 90s suburb, where many of the parents had high-paying jobs, their children went to good schools, played in the woods, and spent their summers at the beach. Even then, the townspeople felt that their way of life was under threat.

I, too, cannot afford a house in a safe American suburb with good schools. But I can think of few things more torturous than being around people who derive a sense of self-importance from the boards and committees they belong to. The clubs and organizations. The pie fundraisers. The performative apology the suburban moms give for starting with store-bought crust. As though someone who bought your $10 pie is going to complain to you afterwards about your crust. The obligatory fall foliage pictures. Only the spiritually broken would fit such a mold.

Maybe that’s the hard truth of working in the home remodeling side of architecture. Your clients are townspeople. You have to listen to them rant that apartments are a threat to their 1950s version of suburban utopia. You feel the fear in their hearts when they’re sitting across the table from you. It oozes into your pores. It drains your vitality. You feel the relief in your whole body when you push open the office doors at 5:15.

Listening to the townspeople talk turns your mind to mush. You won’t go to a cafe and write for a couple of hours. You’ll go home and stare at your four walls and ceiling. Maybe you’ll dilute your writing voice to appease them. Be performatively modest. Not offer your full self. Maybe this is the end. Maybe you don’t have to really go for it.

Transient labor jobs aren’t much different:

“If I were running this place, we’d have a much better menu.” Followed by a rant about the fancy restaurants they worked in before this.

“The front could use a new paint job.”

“I hope the manager’s marriage fails.”

Townspeople are everywhere at all levels of society.

The seatbelt sign rings, and I’m reminded of the few times I really went for it, and what that took. I think about what it takes to forge your own path. It’s not always easy to tell when you’re actively pursuing an aligned life, and when you’re staring at it through the glass.

You retreat, and the townspeople say, “Good to see you’re back in the fold.” They love it when you retreat. It strokes their sorry egos. “Stop by and grab a pint.”

On the plane, I play Fortune Days by The Glitch Mob. A personal 2014-era classic. Maybe I wanted a confirmation that I could still taste that version of myself in the present moment. The song doesn’t resonate emotionally like it once did. The ever-expanding bubble of life has a way of reducing past risk-taking into a mere blip. I’m not my 24-year-old self in February 2015 anymore.

I play Trên Tình Bạn Dưới Tình Yêu by MIN in the plane lavatory. I do my best to avoid the pee dribble in my brand new shoes. For months, I imagined what this song would feel like when I took to the skies. Perhaps I exhausted the newness of the song on those walks to the cafe in the Arizona desert. I packed my dust-stained shoes with me too. I wanted those shoes to see my life working out. I packed the pillow that was with me on all those sleepless nights.

My short layover in Tokyo was a dream. A delirium state. Body dizzy with tiredness, mind too excited to sleep. Another duty-free shop with the same luxury handbag names and chocolates. The international system is comfortably familiar. Still another 6-hour flight to go. I ask what time it is in Phoenix to know when I’m meant to be sleeping. She knows. As does my phone, still in airplane mode.

I’m looking forward, right?

I arrived at my final destination just before midnight. From the rooftop terrace of my airport hotel, I watch the planes take off. Humidity caresses my arms. That familiar sweet taste of air pollution mixed with tropical, dew-soaked vegetation. I could just stay in this quiet village surrounded by rice fields for a few more days. The cafe across the street has a cute tiny dog. He hugs my leg. I think he wants my fried rice with sausage. I know the feeling too well. The “just arrived” glow. Bask in it too long, and the pinhole closes.

I’m still moving. Still passing through it. It’s irreversible now.

In our first meeting, the uplifting MIN song comes on again. I Shazam it to remember the timestamp. 29 October, 2026, 20:45. The rain cloud stops exactly where we’re sitting. The pavement is still dry to our left, wet to our right. I keep my receipt for the two milk teas.

Crossing the street here with all the motorbike traffic is a metaphor for life. Cross with pure conviction without hesitation, and the traffic gracefully moves around you.

I forgive myself for retreating all those years ago. The townspeople’s coercion is comfortable at first. They’ll tell you when you hit the guardrails, and gently nudge you back into the fold. They’re very kind when you fit their mold. It’s all conditional.

Passing through the pinhole is overwhelming at times. There’s a lot to process. It’s disorienting.

It’s not going to turn out as I expected, but I fully trust in what God has in store for us. He is more powerful than we can possibly imagine.

National Express owner Mobico agreed to a Â£308 million takeover from Spain's Autobuses de LeÃ³n, 46p a share, about $413.5 million. Serval raised $150 million in a Sequoia led Series C at a $3 billion valuation, tripling the $1 billion it was worth in December. Its CFO resigned the same week and the stock dropped 6%. Even the biggest buyer has bills in dollars. Hold your own coins and nobody else's obligations come first.

text: 67/100 Practice six: waking up on purpose. The anchor checks where your mind is. Waking up is what you do when you catch it on autopilot. The moment you realise you've been scrolling for twenty minutes, or rehearsing an argument in the shower, or driving with no memory of the last ten kilometres, skip the scolding. Self-criticism just launches a fresh story in the default mode network. Name it lightly instead, almost with a smirk: "Ah. Autopilot." Then make one deliberate micro-choice. Phone face down. Feel the water temperature. Look at one real object for three seconds. Lucid dream research offers a nice parallel. In the 1980s Stephen LaBerge at Stanford showed that some people can realise they're dreaming while still inside the dream and signal it with pre-agreed eye movements. Later work, such as a 2009 study by Ursula Voss and colleagues, found distinctive brain activity in lucid dreams, including more activity in frontal areas. Lucid dreaming is a niche field and no goal of this book. It does give you a powerful image: you can be inside an experience and know at the same time that you're inside it. That double awareness is the whole skill, and the daytime version is available right now, no pillow required.

text:
Some of the best product marketing doesn't feel like marketing at all. It feels like learning something useful.

#Webflow has built an interesting organic growth strategy around this idea.

Someone wants to learn how to build a responsive website. Another person is trying to understand CSS layouts or create their first portfolio site. They start looking for tutorials and discover Webflow University.

They came to learn a skill, but along the way, they also discover a tool they can use to put that knowledge into practice.

Here's what makes this approach work.

01. It attracts people through what they want to learn.

Webflow University offers tutorials and courses on website design, responsive layouts, interactions, and other web development concepts. These topics appeal to people who are actively building their skills, giving them a reason to discover Webflow beyond a typical product search.

02. The education connects directly to the product.

Instead of learning concepts in isolation, users can see how website design principles apply to actual projects. Tutorials help them understand the process while introducing the platform's practical capabilities.

03. Learning reduces the barrier to getting started.

A website builder can feel intimidating to someone who has never designed a website before. Step-by-step lessons make the process more approachable, helping learners build confidence as they become familiar with the tools.

04. The skills create a reason to keep using the product.

Once someone learns to build a landing page, customize a layout, or create a portfolio in Webflow, they have a practical reason to continue using those skills on future projects.

The clever part is how education and product adoption support each other. People discover Webflow because they want to learn, build confidence through its educational resources, and get opportunities to apply what they've learned within the platform.

For SaaS companies, this is a useful way to think about content marketing.

Your audience might not be ready to buy today, but they could be ready to learn something that brings them closer to needing your product.

When your product helps people develop a skill, teaching that skill can become one of your strongest organic acquisition channels.

BREAKING: Anthropic files for IPO after losing $80 BILLION in first half of 2026 | The Post Millennial

AI firm Anthropic, headed by Dario Amodei, is officially heading for an IPO after the company filed paperwork on Monday to be offered on the public market.

In a form filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company plans to be traded on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT." This is despite the tech giant losing $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026.

"Anthropic intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The number of shares of Class A common stock to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering have not yet been determined," the company said in a press release about the S-1 filing.

The AI company, which is behind Claude, filed with the SEC in June confidentially so that the agency could review their financials. The company was founded by CEO Dario Amodei after he as well as other AI researchers left OpenAI. Anthropic has become a go-to for many companies seeking AI tools in corporate America, including the company's Claude Code and Claude Cowork.

The company has been in a race with OpenAI and Google to become the go-to AI platform. Despite its rapid growth, Anthropic CEO Amodei has come under fire for claiming earlier this year that AI companies need to "pace the frontier" with government regulation. Although he called for a slowdown, citing potential catastrophe, Anthropic does not show signs of slowing down anytime soon.

Anthropic's IPO will likely come just months after Elon Musk's SpaceX hit the Nasdaq as the largest IPO on record, which raised $85.7 billion. Although the IPO is expected to be enormous, Anthropic may be entering the public market as investors have grown skittish about a possible pullback on AI spending if investments in the technology do not deliver greater efficiency for corporate customers.

Just four hours short of 24/7 service. Scaling remains the real test.

Customers include IMC Logistics, WattEV, QX Logistics, Einride, and ZET SCALE.

The next milestone: actual production volumes and deliveries.

A London court rejected challenges by X, Meta, and TikTok to Ofcom’s demands for content moderation and online safety data.

X warned compliance could cost millions of pounds.

This was NOT a finding of safety violations or a fine.

4. Neuralink: Telepathy and Blindsight

Telepathy aims to enable high-speed communication through brain signals.

Blindsight aims to restore vision, even for people born blind.

Musk says Blindsight is engineering-ready, pending regulatory approval.

Human results remain unproven.

5. Tesla China Cuts the Upfront Cost of Buying an EV

Tesla reduced minimum down payments on select Model 3 and Model Y financing plans from RMB 79,900 to RMB 39,900.

Five-year, zero-interest financing runs through November 30.

Lower down payments do not mean lower vehicle prices.

6. Tesla Shifts Referral Rewards Toward FSD

Eligible owners can refer someone for a free one-month FSD trial.

If the recipient subscribes, the referrer earns a free FSD month or $99 in Tesla Credits.

U.S. vehicle referral rewards have ended.

Tesla is prioritizing software subscriptions.

7. Starlink Introduces Dynamic Pricing

Starlink Residential prices now vary by local network capacity and demand.

Some areas are seeing prices roughly 20% above or below standard rates.

Changes for certain existing customers begin after November 30.

A new approach to monetizing network capacity.

Musk acknowledged delays in Grok 4.8 development, emphasizing real-world usefulness over benchmark rankings.

Meanwhile, Grok Bot continues moving toward AI agents and enterprise workflows.

No confirmed Grok 4.8 launch date yet.

Compatible Powerwall 3 systems can increase heating when solar generation is abundant or electricity is cheaper.

The goal: reduce consumption during expensive periods.

Tesla is building a more integrated home energy ecosystem.

Musk offered a positive update on Terafab, a key part of his long-term AI chip manufacturing ambitions.

But no new equipment installation, production yield, or manufacturing output figures were disclosed.

Progress claims still need measurable milestones.

11. Cybercab Faces Its NHTSA Response Deadline

October 30 marks Tesla’s deadline to respond to NHTSA’s AQ26002 inquiry into Cybercab safety certification.

No publicly verifiable response was located during this review.

That does NOT establish a missed filing or a regulatory violation.

12. Tesla Announces 36 New Supercharger Sites

Tesla revealed 36 owner-selected Q3 2026 Supercharger locations across 19 markets, including Hanksville, Utah, and Miyazu, Japan.

The global network now exceeds 85,000 stalls at 9,000 sites.

Q4 voting is open.

🌌 The Galaxy has landed—and California LASIK & Eye is first in California.

We’re proud to be the first clinic in California to offer the RayOne Galaxy, bringing a new approach to vision correction to our Sacramento patients. 

https://t.co/ZfVmjZU2cY

What makes this lens different? Artificial intelligence helped design its optics.

According to Rayner, a proprietary AI engine trained on patient outcomes helped develop Galaxy’s distinctive spiral optical design. This is AI used to help engineer the lens itself—not a computer inside your eye, and not simply software used to calculate your prescription. 

https://t.co/5mKYZeOA4O

Rather than relying on the concentric diffractive steps found in many multifocal lenses, Galaxy uses a non-diffractive spiral optic to manage light. Its design aims to deliver a continuous range of vision while minimizing unwanted visual effects such as halos and glare. 

https://t.co/oqSVL5Dac1

The goal: distance, intermediate, and near vision with less dependence on glasses—from looking across the room, to working at a computer, to reading a menu. 

https://t.co/MionFBUsCZ

For me, this is one of the most exciting applications of AI in medicine: not just automating paperwork, but helping us rethink the medical devices we use to care for patients.

At California LASIK & Eye, being first is a milestone. Choosing the right technology for the right patient is the mission.

Galaxy adds another option to that conversation—not a one-size-fits-all solution. Candidacy matters, results vary, and no lens guarantees freedom from glasses or visual side effects. 

AI-assisted design. Physician-guided care. A new Galaxy of possibilities.

#VoteRedToSaveAmerica 

Remember when Abigail Spanberger told everyone she grew up around gun owners, carried a firearm every day as a federal agent, and supported the Second Amendment? Well, she got elected governor of Virginia, and within months she was signed almost two dozen gun restrictions into law, including a ban on future sales of semiautomatic firearms and magazines holding more than 15 rounds. She talked about respecting gun ownership, but she also supported new gun restrictions before the election. Now Virginia gun owners are fighting some of those laws in court.

And here she is with Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, whose campaign has already publicly supported red flag laws and stronger background checks. The Second Amendment says “shall not be infringed,” and the debate over what that means has real consequences for millions of Americans. Virginia offers a clear example of how quickly firearm laws can change after an election. Ohio voters deserve to know precisely where their candidates stand before casting their ballots but Acton refused to debate, interview, or even allow cameras around when she talks. Scary.
